prompt: Policy classes and export classes import each other; both teams change the classification for one export. What first separates that cyclic dependency?

options.text: Use a shared classification contract with one-way imports.
Keep the cycle and add a runtime null check.
Put both classes in a larger package so imports look local.
Copy the classification rule into both classes.

feedback.reason: The cycle comes from mutual compile-time knowledge of one decision.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A contract can break an import cycle while the runtime collaboration remains in both directions if needed.
details.scenarioApplication: The two packages co-change the same export classification and currently import one another.
details.errorCorrection: A null check addresses runtime values, not the source dependency cycle.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A new contract helps only if it is independently owned and does not re-import either implementation.
details.transfer: When two modules need each other’s types, isolate the shared contract at the stable decision boundary.

messages.text: The null check cannot remove either import edge.
Moving both classes together hides the cycle without changing the dependency graph.
Duplicated rules can diverge after the next classification change.

prompt: Order policy owns settlement decisions; Payment only reports status. The modules mutually import each other only to exchange that result. Which change breaks the cycle without moving the decision?

options.text: Keep the result with order policy; payment returns it.
Move the whole payment workflow into order processing.
Let both modules publish copies of the result structure.
Have order processing import payment internals through a shared barrel.

feedback.reason: Order policy owns settlement semantics, so the shared result contract belongs at that policy boundary.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A policy-owned result type can break the source cycle while payment still reports its provider status through the agreed boundary.
details.scenarioApplication: Order policy decides settlement meaning; Payment reports status and returns the result in the Order-owned contract.
details.errorCorrection: Moving the workflow transfers payment responsibility, not just the shared type.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Keep the contract small and stable; do not create a general shared package for unrelated types.
details.transfer: A result used by one policy should normally be shaped around that policy’s needs.

messages.text: Moving payment orchestration would change which module owns the workflow, not just the result contract.
Two copied result definitions can drift and still do not establish one contract.
A barrel re-export does not change which implementation the source depends on.

prompt: A `Shared` package contains date formatting, invoice tax rules, and badge authorization. Only date formatting is used by all three consumers; policy changes force unrelated rebuilds. What boundary is justified?

options.text: Share formatting; keep tax and badge rules with their policies.
Move all three into each consumer to eliminate every dependency.
Keep one package because any reuse proves the concepts cohere.
Create one service per function even though the rules change together with their policies.

feedback.reason: Reuse alone does not make unrelated rules one cohesive module.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Cohesion follows a shared reason to change, while a narrow stable utility may still be shared.
details.scenarioApplication: The facts distinguish one cross-cutting representation helper from two policy-specific rules.
details.errorCorrection: Copying every utility creates needless duplication and still does not identify the policy boundaries.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Avoid splitting a cohesive policy into one-function services without an independent change boundary.
details.transfer: Group code by the decisions that change together, not by a general `shared` label.

messages.text: This copies the shared formatter along with policy logic without evidence that all three need separate copies.
A single consumer of a reusable helper does not make unrelated tax and access policies cohesive.
The scenario says each rule changes with its owning policy; one-function services add boundaries without evidence.

prompt: Checkout imports Gateway; Gateway imports Checkout solely to use Checkout.Request during a callback. Which dependency refactor best preserves who starts the use case?

options.text: Give Gateway a Checkout-owned callback contract.
Move the checkout use case into Gateway.
Use a dynamic import from Gateway back to Checkout.
Duplicate Checkout.Request in Gateway and cast between the two.

feedback.reason: The back edge exists only because the provider names a caller-owned request type.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A boundary contract removes the compile-time back edge without reversing runtime control.
details.scenarioApplication: Checkout still initiates payment; the gateway calls the supplied contract on completion.
details.errorCorrection: Moving the use case changes who owns orchestration; dynamic loading only postpones the same dependency.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Choose a minimal callback shape instead of exporting the whole checkout module.
details.transfer: Runtime callbacks can point toward the caller even when compile-time dependencies point toward abstractions.

messages.text: Gateway owning checkout orchestration would change responsibility not required by the callback.
Dynamic import delays loading but retains a dependency from Gateway to Checkout.
A copied type has no shared type identity and needs a conversion boundary anyway.

prompt: Invoice depends on Money, TaxPolicy, and CustomerStatus. The graph has no cycle, and all three change for different reasons. Which conclusion follows?

options.text: Keep the acyclic edges absent a concrete boundary problem.
Split every imported type into its own package to reduce edge count.
Merge all four modules because an acyclic graph means one cohesive module.
Create a mediator solely to hide the three dependency edges.

feedback.reason: Acyclicity and cohesion answer different questions.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Acyclic dependency structure can still contain several useful directed boundaries.
details.scenarioApplication: The graph has no cycle and each dependency has an independently stated change reason.
details.errorCorrection: Splitting every type would increase coordination without removing a demonstrated problem.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Do not infer that a graph is wrong merely because a module has several dependencies.
details.transfer: Use cycle evidence to break cycles and co-change/client evidence to reconsider cohesion.

messages.text: One package per type does not follow from the supplied evidence.
No cycle does not prove the modules share one reason to change.
Hiding edges behind a mediator preserves the underlying policy dependencies.

prompt: Scheduling rules change together, but the dashboard only reads their published schedule result. Where should the boundary sit?

options.text: Keep the co-changing rules together; expose their result.
Split each rule because the dashboard reads a result.
Make the dashboard import every rule implementation.
Copy all scheduling rules into the dashboard.

feedback.reason: A read-only client of a result does not need to participate in the policy module’s internal cohesion.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A module can keep co-changing rules together while presenting a separate outward contract.
details.scenarioApplication: The rule set changes as one policy; the dashboard consumes only its result.
details.errorCorrection: Splitting each rule would make their shared change coordinated across packages.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The result contract should not expose rule internals unless a client requirement needs them.
details.transfer: Separate internal cohesion from the shape of a module’s public output.

messages.text: The stated co-change is evidence to keep the rules together.
The dashboard needs only the published result, not each implementation.
Copying the policy creates a second rule set that can drift.

prompt: AccessPolicy and BadgeStore import each other: policy uses the store, while store imports AccessDecision to serialize it. What is the narrowest cycle-breaking move?

options.text: Map the decision to a store-owned persistence representation.
Move authorization into BadgeStore.
Make AccessPolicy import the store’s database entity.
Add a third package that imports both concrete modules.

feedback.reason: Persistence representation is creating the back edge from storage into policy.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Mapping at the persistence adapter keeps policy decisions independent of the stored schema.
details.scenarioApplication: BadgeStore only needs a stable representation to persist the policy result.
details.errorCorrection: Moving authorization changes its owner; importing the database entity reverses the dependency.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The stored representation need not be the domain decision object.
details.transfer: Keep policy and persistence models separate when their change reasons differ.

messages.text: BadgeStore would then own a decision that the scenario assigns to AccessPolicy.
Importing the database entity deepens the dependency on storage details.
A third package importing both does not break the concrete imports between them.

prompt: Search has two interchangeable engines. Both teams agree the request/result shape changes only when the search capability changes; ranking rules change independently. What should the contract contain?

options.text: Publish a stable search request and result contract.
Every engine configuration and ranking field so callers can optimize each provider.
Only a marker interface with no callable contract.
A shared model containing all search and ranking types.

feedback.reason: A useful boundary captures the stable capability, not all implementation knobs.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A narrow interface enables substitution while keeping unrelated policy changes local.
details.scenarioApplication: Engine implementations vary, but callers need a stable query and result shape.
details.errorCorrection: Provider configuration would couple callers to volatile implementation details.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Do not erase behavior from the contract if callers need to express a query.
details.transfer: Model the capability callers use and keep independently changing ranking policy separate.

messages.text: Provider-specific knobs make the shared interface vary with each engine.
A marker gives no operation through which the caller can use the capability.
The shared model would couple two independently changing concepts.

prompt: Parser and Importer form a source cycle because each imports the other’s types, although Importer only needs a parsed-record result. What boundary fits?

options.text: Give Importer a stable parsed-record input contract.
Make Parser own the entire import workflow.
Let each side keep a private incompatible copy of the result.
Combine Parser and Importer into one file while retaining their mutual abstractions.

feedback.reason: The back edge comes from a result type crossing a boundary without clear ownership.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A caller-facing result contract can be shared without exposing parser internals.
details.scenarioApplication: Importer consumes records; it does not need Parser’s implementation types.
details.errorCorrection: Owning the workflow in Parser expands its responsibility beyond parsing.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If they are actually one cohesive unit, merge the module; otherwise a filename change is not a contract fix.
details.transfer: Break cycles at a stable exchanged concept, not by hiding imports.

messages.text: Parser owning the full workflow collapses two responsibilities without evidence.
Private copies cannot guarantee the same shape at the boundary.
One file does not remove the two-way type dependency.

prompt: Three unrelated packages import `Logging.Common`; only a small adapter actually calls the logger, while domain packages merely import its helpers. What is the safest first cohesion move?

options.text: Remove unused domain imports; keep logging at the adapter.
Move domain rules into Logging.Common because it is already widely imported.
Create one logging package per domain type.
Replace every import with a global singleton.

feedback.reason: Import popularity is not evidence that a package owns the importing policies.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Removing unused edges improves cohesion without introducing new ownership claims.
details.scenarioApplication: The domain packages do not call logging; the adapter does.
details.errorCorrection: Moving rules into Logging.Common follows dependency count rather than responsibility.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If domain code needs a logging capability, define the smallest boundary required by that use.
details.transfer: Inspect actual use and co-change before changing package ownership.

messages.text: A common dependency does not make logging the owner of domain decisions.
One package per type adds boundaries unsupported by the scenario.
A global singleton hides the dependency instead of removing it.

prompt: RefundUseCase and RefundPolicy import each other: the use case asks for eligibility; the policy imports the use case to construct its result. Which refactor maintains the policy boundary?

options.text: Let RefundPolicy return a policy-owned eligibility result; RefundUseCase interprets it.
Move eligibility rules into RefundUseCase and delete the policy module.
Let the policy return a use-case class instance.
Create a shared package of all use-case and policy classes.

feedback.reason: The result should express a policy decision without naming the orchestration class.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A policy-owned result permits the use case to depend on the policy contract in one direction.
details.scenarioApplication: RefundPolicy determines eligibility; RefundUseCase coordinates the operation.
details.errorCorrection: A use-case object in the policy result recreates the back dependency.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Keep the result sufficient for orchestration but independent of UI and workflow details.
details.transfer: Business policy should return its own decision vocabulary to the caller.

messages.text: Deleting the policy moves its explicitly separate eligibility responsibility.
Returning a use-case instance retains the cycle through a different type.
A shared package may centralize classes but does not define a one-way dependency.

prompt: Library and Gym each change their access rules for separate regulators; a shared `AccessRules` package changes in every release for either client. What package boundary reduces unrelated coordination?

options.text: Keep each regulator’s rules local; share stable mechanics only.
Keep both policies together because both use the word access.
Copy the shared mechanics and all rule code into every caller.
Make the regulator import both client modules.

feedback.reason: Different change authorities are concrete evidence against one shared policy package.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Cohesion follows the responsibility and change reason; common mechanics can remain a separate stable dependency.
details.scenarioApplication: The two rule sets respond to different regulator changes.
details.errorCorrection: A name similarity does not make their policies one decision.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Share only mechanics that do not vary with either regulator’s policy.
details.transfer: When change reasons diverge, separate policy even if the domain vocabulary overlaps.

messages.text: A common noun alone does not show a single cohesion boundary.
Copying mechanics and policy creates synchronization work with no stated benefit.
The regulator is not a module responsible for either client’s internal policy.

prompt: Domain owns the stable policy operation; Infrastructure owns the vendor transaction and calls that operation. The database transaction type is imported into Domain only for that handling. Which boundary change fits these responsibilities?

options.text: Keep the vendor transaction in Infrastructure; call the Domain policy contract.
Move the policy into Infrastructure so it can use the transaction type.
Make Domain import the complete database client.
Duplicate transaction interfaces in both modules.

feedback.reason: Infrastructure owns the vendor transaction, while Domain owns the stable policy operation.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A one-way policy contract lets Infrastructure handle its transaction mechanism without importing that vendor type into Domain.
details.scenarioApplication: Infrastructure calls the Domain operation and keeps its database transaction representation local.
details.errorCorrection: Moving the policy or importing the full database client would reverse the stated ownership boundary.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: This selects a source boundary; transaction behavior remains the responsibility of the Infrastructure implementation described in the prompt.
details.transfer: Keep an explicitly owned volatile mechanism at its owner while callers depend on the stable operation contract.

messages.text: Moving the policy follows the volatile mechanism instead of stable rules.
Importing the client deepens the same dependency on infrastructure.
Duplicated contracts can disagree and do not remove the direction problem.

prompt: UsageAnalysis computes metrics, uploads files, emails owners, and renders a dashboard. These change for separate product reasons. What module split is justified?

options.text: Separate responsibilities with independent change triggers.
Keep them together because every report uses all four actions.
Split every method into a package even when two methods change together.
Move metrics into the email client because it starts the workflow.

feedback.reason: The stated change reasons are distinct and the methods cross several responsibilities.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Cohesion is improved by grouping operations that change for the same reason.
details.scenarioApplication: Metrics, upload provider, email policy, and display requirements vary separately.
details.errorCorrection: A workflow’s sequential use does not make its components one responsibility.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Do not split further without evidence that another responsibility changes independently.
details.transfer: Use actual reasons to change, not call sequence alone, to choose boundaries.

messages.text: Sequential use alone does not establish one reason to change.
One method per package adds boundaries beyond the independent reasons stated.
Starting the workflow does not make the email provider owner of metrics.

prompt: OrderPolicy and MessageBus cycle through an event type used to announce an accepted order. Which dependency direction keeps policy independent of transport?

options.text: Let policy define the event; let the adapter publish it.
Make OrderPolicy import the bus SDK event class.
Move acceptance rules into MessageBus.
Copy the event type into both modules and translate implicitly.

feedback.reason: The event’s business meaning is stable while the transport implementation varies.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A transport adapter can map a policy-level event into a bus-specific message.
details.scenarioApplication: OrderPolicy decides acceptance; MessageBus transports the resulting event.
details.errorCorrection: Using the SDK event class couples the policy to transport choices.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Only publish data the receiving side needs; do not expose all policy internals.
details.transfer: Let the stable decision own its event meaning and let adapters own wire formats.

messages.text: SDK classes make the policy depend on transport details.
Moving acceptance to the bus reverses responsibility.
Separate copies require a mapping and can drift.

prompt: Several packages import `DateCommon` for formatting, billing cutoffs, and entitlement expiry. The last two use different time-zone and calendar rules. What should be separated?

options.text: Share formatting; separate cutoff and expiry policies.
Keep every date decision in DateCommon because each uses a date.
Duplicate the formatter separately inside every consumer.
Merge Billing and Entitlement because both compare timestamps.

feedback.reason: A common data type does not prove the decisions around it are cohesive.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A utility can share representation work while domain-specific policies remain independent.
details.scenarioApplication: Formatting changes cross consumers; cutoff and expiry semantics have different owners.
details.errorCorrection: Putting policy in DateCommon ties unrelated domains to a generic utility.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Share a function only where behavior and change reason are actually shared.
details.transfer: Separate shared syntax from rules that interpret it.

messages.text: A shared primitive does not establish one calendar policy.
Duplicating the common formatter adds maintenance without solving the policy split.
Both use timestamps, but their rules change for different product reasons.

prompt: Report depends on ArchiveStore and LiveStore; both implement Report’s stable read contract. There is no reverse import. What should be done about the graph?

options.text: Keep the acyclic direction until a concrete problem appears.
Introduce a mediator to make the graph appear symmetrical.
Merge all three modules because both stores serve reports.
Invert the report so each store imports its use case.

feedback.reason: The graph already has the desired one-way dependency and no stated change pressure.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Directed dependencies need not be symmetric.
details.scenarioApplication: Report consumes a read abstraction and the stores implement it.
details.errorCorrection: A mediator would add another edge and concept without solving a cycle.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Revisit only if report policy and storage representation begin changing together.
details.transfer: Do not refactor a healthy acyclic graph solely for visual symmetry.

messages.text: Symmetry is not a dependency-quality requirement.
Serving one consumer does not mean the stores and report have one change reason.
Making the stores depend on report orchestration reverses a useful boundary.

prompt: DocumentTools combines redaction policy and PDF rendering; redaction rules change with legal review while rendering changes with a vendor SDK. What boundary is warranted?

options.text: Separate redaction policy from the PDF rendering adapter.
Move redaction into the PDF adapter because it handles the document bytes.
Put the SDK and legal rules in one package to reduce imports.
Copy redaction rules into each renderer.

feedback.reason: The two responsibilities have different stated change authorities.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A policy can select what is redacted while an adapter handles the rendering mechanism.
details.scenarioApplication: Legal review changes redaction; the vendor SDK changes rendering.
details.errorCorrection: The renderer’s access to bytes does not make it the owner of legal policy.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Keep the handoff explicit so policy remains testable without provider-specific types.
details.transfer: Separate decisions that change for different reasons and connect them through a narrow capability.

messages.text: Byte access does not determine ownership of redaction rules.
One package would couple legal policy to a volatile SDK.
Duplicated policy can produce inconsistent redaction across renderers.
